criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural household access to piped drinking water on premises from the general network across Brazilian municipalities between 2000 and 2010.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study clearly examines institutional, governance, and administrative arrangements in rural water service provision (decentralized municipal provision vs. community water user associations, regional state-owned utilities, municipal user-participation mechanisms, and local political accountability). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, although parts of the paper frame the intervention around participatory vs. non-participatory project choice and political-economy accountability channels (media, elections, social pressure groups), the core exposure recorded in IBGE's National Basic Sanitation Survey (PNSB) and explored in the qualitative interviews is the legal/institutional service-provider and ownership structure governing ongoing rural piped water supply: water user associations (often operating under municipal concession contracts or formal co-investment conditions) implementing, operating, and maintaining systems versus local municipal governments/public firms (alongside models testing local municipal vs. regional state-owned CESB main utility ownership and switches). This falls directly within utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary and secondary empirical evidence combining quantitative panel econometrics (multinomial probit kernel propensity-score matching with difference-in-differences across 2000-2010 using Brazilian Demographic Census, PNSB, and Ipeadata) and 36 semi-structured telephone interviews with municipal officials, water user association presidents, regional water company representatives, and sector experts.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports municipal rural piped-water access rates (share of the rural population with piped drinking water on premises from the general network in 2000 and 2010, and the 2000-2010 change in access rates).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (Brazilian municipalities and their rural populations, N = 1,008 matched project municipalities / 1,899 municipality-year observations in the main kernel-weighted DiD and up to 5,389 municipalities / 10,448 observations in unweighted DiD, plus 36 sector interviewees), exposure (provider/ownership type of new rural small-scale water systems in 2000-2008: water user association vs. local municipal government/public provider, plus main-supplier ownership and accountability moderators), outcome (rural piped water on premises access rate change, 2000-2010), and study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English, an eligible review language without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper investigates whether small-scale water supply systems implemented and operated by water user associations increase access to piped water supply in rural Brazil by more than systems by local governments.
In most cases, the local government only signs a concession contract to transfer responsibility for water supply to the association.

Such providers can be regional ﬁrms (CESB), local municipality governments or local (public) ﬁrms owned by the municipality, water user associations, private supply ﬁrms, and intermunicipal or interfederal cooperations.

As the eﬀect of project type on access rates might be confounded by simultaneous drivers of project-type choice and access rates, the quantitative analysis is based on a diﬀerence-in-diﬀerence estimator in combination with kernel matching to overcome the endogeneity of project type.
Table 1 shows access rates to piped water on premises from the general network in Brazil in the year 2000 and their increase from 2000 to the year 2010.

raw_response.exposure: Institutional provider and ownership/management structure of small-scale rural water supply systems introduced during 2000-2008: community water user associations (often delegated responsibility via municipal concession contracts) implementing, operating, and maintaining supply systems versus local municipal governments or municipal public firms (as well as regional state-owned CESB vs. local municipal main utility ownership, formal municipal participation mechanisms, and local political accountability channels).
raw_response.outcome: Access rate (proportion of rural residents) to piped drinking water on premises from the general network in 2000 and 2010, and the 2000-2010 percentage-point increase in rural piped-water access rates at the municipality level.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Brazilian municipalities (unit of analysis: municipality-year rural areas; 4,892 municipalities in descriptive comparison, 1,008 matched project municipalities / 1,899 observations in main kernel-weighted DiD, and up to 5,389 municipalities / 10,448 observations in full-sample DiD), supplemented by 36 semi-structured interviews (22 municipal representatives, 3 water user association presidents, 4 academic/government sector experts, and 7 regional water firm representatives).
raw_response.rationale: Barde (2017) is an empirical mixed-methods panel study in English evaluating how utility/provider ownership and management structure for small-scale rural water supply systems in Brazil (community water user associations operating systems—often via municipal concession contracts—versus local municipal government/public firm providers, alongside local vs. regional state-owned CESB main suppliers) affects rural household piped-water connection rates between 2000 and 2010. It satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access).
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods longitudinal panel study combining kernel-weighted propensity-score matching and difference-in-differences estimation (2000-2010 municipal panel) with 36 semi-structured stakeholder interviews
